sections.html: A launch checklist item "public endpoint has per-identity token limits" appeared only after an anonymous endpoint turned into someone's free chat backend over one weekend.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests only rate limiting, no cost math.
  • Hire: computes per-call and per-hour damage, adds auth, token quotas, caps and a kill switch.
  • Strong hire: also covers prompt injection, caching by URL, anomaly alerting, provider-side spend caps and a lasting launch-review rule.

questions.promptHtml: How do you tie LLM cost to business metrics, forecast it, and make sure a cost-cutting change does not just break quality?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-level engineers own the margin, not only the code. The signal is unit economics plus a quality gate on every saving.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I track cost per active user, per resolved ticket and per document, and gross margin by plan, because total spend alone hides whether the feature is healthy. I forecast with users x actions per user x tokens per action, add growth and seasonality plus a safety margin, and recheck against real data after launch. Every cost cut must pass the quality eval, otherwise it is a bug that saves money, and I count downstream costs such as retries and human escalations.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Unit economics example (illustrative): support bot costs $0.12 per conversation, resolves 70 percent without a human; each escalation costs $4 of agent time. Per 100 conversations: LLM $12, escalations 30 x $4 = $120, so total $132, i.e. $1.32 per conversation. A cheaper model that costs $0.06 but resolves 60 percent: LLM $6, escalations 40 x $4 = $160, total $166: cost went up 26 percent. The LLM bill fell, the total cost rose.

Forecast: tokens = users x actions/user x tokens/action, then dollars. Add growth, seasonality, a safety margin (say 20 to 30 percent) and revisit after launch. Negotiate committed-use discounts only after usage stabilizes, otherwise you commit to the wrong volume.

Governance: every new feature gets a cost estimate before launch; weekly review of cost per unit; pricing and quotas tied to the numbers (free tier, usage-based pricing for heavy users).

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not needed; the worked arithmetic above is the point. A spreadsheet or small script with the formula users x actions x tokens x price is enough.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Optimizing the LLM line while total cost per outcome rises.
  • Forecasting from the pilot cohort, which uses the product differently from the mass market.
  • Committing to volume discounts early.
  • Measuring cost without a quality metric next to it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you gate a cost-cut? → Offline eval on a held-out set plus an online A/B on quality and escalation rate, with a rollback trigger.
  2. What would you put on the dashboard? → Cost per outcome, cache hit rate, calls per request, p95 run cost, spend by feature and tenant.
  3. How do you set pricing? → Use cost per active user at the 90th percentile to price tiers so heavy users do not eat margin.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "reduce tokens." Senior: frames cost as cost per outcome including human escalations, forecasts with margins, gates every saving by an eval, and links pricing to unit economics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team celebrated a 50 percent LLM cost cut and then saw ticket escalations climb; total cost per resolved ticket was higher until the change was partly reverted.

questions.contextHtml: A summarization-and-Q&A product on a single frontier model costs $52,000/month. Breakdown from instrumentation: 55 percent is a "meeting summary" feature (long transcripts, 30k input tokens, 700 output, mostly nightly), 30 percent is interactive Q&A (6k input of which 4.5k is a shared knowledge-base prefix, 250 output), 15 percent is a classification step (500 input, 20 output) that uses the same frontier model. The CEO asks for a 60 percent cut by next quarter without a visible quality drop. Illustrative price $3 in / $15 out per MTok; batch is 50 percent off; cached reads 10 percent.
questions.promptHtml: Present a plan with expected savings per component and the risks.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move everything to the cheapest model." No per-component math, no quality gates, and it breaks the interactive path.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the quality metric per feature and the acceptable regression? Is the nightly summary actually deadline-bound? What is the Q&A latency SLO? What is the labeled data volume for the classifier?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No incident, so first the free wins that do not change the model: batch and caching.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) meeting summary is the largest line and is deferrable, so batch gives a clean 50 percent; (b) Q&A prefix caching saves most of the input cost; (c) the classifier is over-modeled; (d) output trimming matters little.
  4. How I'd verify: Meeting summary $28,600: batch saves 50 percent = $14,300. Q&A $15,600: input is 6k x $3 = $0.018 of which 4.5k is shared; with caching, 4.5k x 0.1 x $3 = $0.00135 versus $0.0135, saving $0.01215 per call of about $0.0225 total (input $0.018 + output $0.00375 = $0.02175); about 56 percent saving, so around $8,700 saved. Classifier $7,800: a small model or fine-tuned classifier at roughly 1/10 the price saves about $7,000. Total savings about $14,300 + $8,700 + $7,000 = $30,000, about 58 percent, close to the target, and I would find the rest in summary trimming (chunk and summarize with a cheaper model, then merge).
  5. Root cause: One model and one mode of operation for three very different workloads.
  6. Fix: Sequence by savings and risk: caching (no quality risk, a day of work), batch for nightly summaries (low risk, needs job tracking), classifier replacement (needs eval and shadow period), then summary tiering. Report each result with a re-measured bill.
  7. Prevention: Per-feature budgets, cost per outcome dashboard, an eval gate in CI on prompts and models.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not replace the classifier before a shadow run shows agreement above the bar. I would not promise 60 percent before measuring cache hit rates, since my estimates assume near-perfect hits.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the nightly summaries must arrive by 7 am? → Batch window risk; submit early, keep real-time fallback for stragglers.
  • What if cache hit rate is 50 percent? → Q&A savings halve; recompute and tell the CEO the forecast changed.
  • What if quality drops 1 point on summaries? → Is it visible? Use human review on a sample, accept if within the agreed band, otherwise keep the larger model for long transcripts only.

sections.html:
def saving(monthly, factor): return monthly * (1 - factor)

plan = {"summary_batch": saving(28600, 0.5),
        "qa_cache": 15600 * 0.56,
        "classifier": 7800 * 0.9}
print(round(sum(plan.values())), "per month")   # ~30,000 of 52,000
val plan = mapOf(
    "summary_batch" to 28600 * 0.5,
    "qa_cache" to 15600 * 0.56,
    "classifier" to 7800 * 0.9)
fun main() = println(plan.values.sum())   // about 30,000 of 52,000
static double totalSaving() {
    return 28600 * 0.5 + 15600 * 0.56 + 7800 * 0.9;   // about 30,000 of 52,000 per month
}

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promised 60 percent cut landed at 41 percent because the cache hit rate in production was 70 percent, not the 100 percent assumed; the plan survived because each component was measured and reported separately.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: switches model globally, no per-component math.
  • Hire: breaks down the bill, applies batch, caching and classifier replacement with arithmetic and quality checks.
  • Strong hire: sequences by risk, states assumptions (hit rate, batch deadline), reports honestly against the target and sets ongoing governance.
